title: IRSA: a pod with a role instead of a static key

videos.script: A pod in your cluster needs to read a bucket. The quickest way is an access key in a Kubernetes secret. It works on the first afternoon, and it is wrong on every day after it. {{key}} This lesson starts with why. A static key never expires. It gets copied into places nobody tracks. And every pod that holds it looks like the same user. {{trust}} Then it builds the replacement. Every EKS cluster has an identity provider of its own. You tell IAM to believe it. Then you write a role that trusts one service account, and nothing else. {{exchange}} After that you watch the exchange itself. The pod hands a token to STS, and gets back credentials that last an hour. You run it on your own laptop, with the same two variables a pod is given. moto plays STS here, and it believes any token at all. AWS checks the signature, and the lesson says exactly what it checks. {{identity}} The last section is the newer way, EKS Pod Identity. An agent on each node does the exchange, and no identity provider is needed. You will run a small stand-in for that agent, and see what the SDK asks it for.
